newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: U.N. war crimes court to deliver first judgement.
newsitem.headline: U.N. war crimes court to deliver first judgement.

text.p: The U.N. war crimes tribunal for former Yugoslavia will rule on Wednesday whether a Bosnian Serb police reservist is guilty of torturing and killing Moslems during a Serb "ethnic cleansing" campaign in Bosnia in 1992.
The U.N. tribunals for Yugoslavia and Rwanda mark the first attempt to try war criminals before an international panel of judges since the Nuremberg and Tokyo trials after World War Two.
The judgement in the case of Dusan "Dusko" Tadic will be the tribunal's first in a full-length trial and will be handed down exactly one year after he went on trial.

Dozens of witnesses told the tribunal last year they had seen Tadic rounding up his former Moslem neighbours in the Prijedor region of northwest Bosnia and roaming the Serb-run prison camps in which they were kept in inhuman conditions.
But only a handful said they had seen the former bar-owner, karate enthusiast and father of two girls take part in some of the worst alleged atrocities in the notorious Omarska camp.
Prosecutors allege that Tadic beat, raped and murdered Moslem inmates at Omarska and other camps as part of a brutal Serb campaign to drive Moslems away from their homes.
Tadic, 41, has always denied the charges and defence lawyers said he had been a hapless victim of Moslems' desire to find a scapegoat for their suffering at the hands of the Serbs.
Tadic's brother Ljubo reiterated this claim in an interview with Reuters correspondent Dan de Luce and the Dutch newspaper Drentse Courant on Monday.
"It's my personal opinion that Dusko, as a Serb, was used to shame the Serb people," he said.
Arrested in Germany in February 1994 while visiting relatives, Tadic has now spent more than three years in custody.
He faces a maximum sentence of life imprisonment as the tribunal, set up by the U.N. Security Council in May 1993, is not allowed to impose the death penalty.
Although the three trial judges will determine his guilt or innocence on Wednesday, their sentence, if they find him guilty, will be announced separately at a later date.
Sentencing will be postponed if, as expected, the prosecution or the defence appeals against the verdict.
Defence lawyers have argued that Tadic was a victim of mistaken identity or of a conspiracy by Moslems to incriminate him.
On many of the occasions when he was alleged to have been committing atrocities, they said, he had been performing routine police traffic duties.
Ljubo Tadic told Reuters it was common knowledge in the Prijedor region that two former policemen had murdered a Moslem whom Tadic has been accused of killing.

Human rights workers said whatever verdict emerged in the Tadic case, those suspected of orchestrating the ethnic cleansing of Moslems in Prijedor remained firmly in power, some of them profiting from international aid to Bosnia.

U.S. prosecutor Brenda Hollis in closing arguments last November said Tadic had been a fervent Serb nationalist who had willingly played an active role in a systematic persecution of Moslems and taken a perverse delight in torture and killing.

Faced with thousands of pages of documentary evidence and the direct testimony of over 100 witnesses, presiding judge Gabrielle Kirk McDonald and her fellow judges from Malaysia and Australia had a duty to convict Tadic, Hollis said.
Tadic is one of eight war crimes suspects held at the Hague tribunal's 24-cell detention centre, though indictments have been issued against 75 suspects to date.
The former Bosnian Serb political and military leaders, Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic, both indicted for genocide against the Bosnian Moslems, are among those still at large.
Authorities in various parts of the former Yugoslavia have given only limited cooperation to the tribunal while NATO-led peacekeepers have refused to hunt down and arrest suspects.
